USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

A chronic oral finding

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A 19-year-old man has taken phenytoin for several years. At a dental visit, he is found to have enlarged gingival tissue around multiple teeth. He has no fever or acute ulceration. Which medication-associated adverse effect best explains this finding?

  1. Corticosteroid-induced oral candidiasis
  2. Gingival hyperplasia
  3. Agranulocytosis proven by inspection alone
  4. Opioid-induced xerostomia
  5. Acute cholinergic poisoning
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Gingival hyperplasia

Chronic phenytoin exposure can cause gingival overgrowth; oral hygiene and dental follow-up are important.

Understanding the options

Gingival hyperplasia
Chronic phenytoin exposure can cause gingival overgrowth; oral hygiene and dental follow-up are important.
Agranulocytosis proven by inspection alone
Blood testing, not gingival appearance alone, is needed to diagnose agranulocytosis.
Opioid-induced xerostomia
The patient is not described as taking an opioid and has tissue overgrowth.
Acute cholinergic poisoning
This would produce an acute secretory syndrome.
Corticosteroid-induced oral candidiasis
Candidiasis typically causes plaques rather than this characteristic enlargement.
